name: v0.73.1
body:
# PageSift 0.73.1 Release Notes: A Shared MCP Service That Reports Its Own Mistakes

> **Release Version**: `v0.73.1`
> **Release Date**: 2026-10-26
> **License**: AGPL-3.0-only (Commercial licensing available)

---

## Overview

0.73.1 makes `pagesift mcp http` fit to run as one long-lived service shared by every AI agent on
a machine, and turns the traffic it serves into bug reports:

- **10× faster MCP calls over HTTP.** Every call on a kept-alive connection waited about 40 ms
  for a TCP delayed ACK; that wait is gone.
- **Audit log.** One JSON line per fetch, HTML snapshots of suspicious results, and a
  `pagesift_report_issue` tool for agents to record wrong results.
- **Cache and warnings in MCP.** `mcp http` uses the configured cache, and the scrape tool tells
  agents when its result may be incomplete.
- **Clean shutdown.** `SIGTERM` closes the browser pool before the process exits.

Setup guide: [Running pagesift as a shared MCP service](https://github.com/YOLOW92/pagesift/blob/v0.73.1/docs/mcp-service.md).

---

## 40 ms per MCP call

The MCP server writes a response as headers followed by a chunked body. With Nagle's algorithm
on, the second small write waited for the client's delayed ACK, so every call on a kept-alive
connection — which is how agents talk to an MCP server — took at least 40 ms however fast the
page was. The MCP and API servers now set `TCP_NODELAY` on every connection.

`pagesift_scrape` over MCP HTTP on a local site, alternating 0.73.0 and 0.73.1, three rounds
(i7-10700, 8 cores / 16 threads):

| Concurrent clients | 0.73.0 req/s | 0.73.1 req/s | 0.73.0 p50 | 0.73.1 p50 |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 26 | 256–266 | 41.0 ms | 3.0–3.1 ms |
| 4 | 104–105 | 907–1145 | 41.0 ms | 2.9–3.5 ms |
| 16 | 415 | 2065–2343 | 41.0 ms | 5.5–6.1 ms |

Requests per second: higher is better; latency: lower is better. CPU time per request (lower is
better, median of four rounds): MCP 3,805 → 3,584 µs, `serve` 3,673 → 3,677 µs, so `serve`
throughput is unchanged; its run-to-run spread on this machine is about ±15%.

---

## Audit log

`--audit-log <path>` on any command, or in `pagesift.toml`:

```toml
[audit]
path = "/home/me/.local/state/pagesift/audit.jsonl"
# max_mb = 64            rotate to <path>.1 past this size
# snapshots = true       keep HTML of suspicious results
# snapshot_dir = "…"     default: snapshots/ next to the log
# snapshot_max_kb = 2048
# snapshots_per_day = 200
# redact = true          strip URL credentials and secret-looking query values
```

Each fetch — single scrapes, batch pages, crawl pages, MCP calls — appends one line with the
source (`mcp-http`, `serve`, `scrape`…), the MCP client's name, URL, final URL, engine and
browser engine, status, content type, cache state, time, extracted characters, HTML size,
warnings, error code and the anti-bot rule that matched. Page text is not logged.

A result is marked `suspicious` when it carries a content warning (`empty_content`,
`thin_content`, `render_unavailable`, `render_skipped_*`), when an HTML page returns 200 with
under 200 characters of text, or when the fetch fails for a reason that is not the caller's
(robots, invalid URLs, private addresses and unsupported options are not counted). Suspicious
results get a snapshot of the HTML pagesift worked from — the rendered DOM when a browser was
used — so the problem can be replayed after the page has changed.

With an audit log configured, the MCP server also offers `pagesift_report_issue` (URL, expected,
actual, optional parameters and note). Reports go into the same log as `kind: "report"`; nothing
leaves the machine.

Cost: CPU per request with the audit log and snapshots on was within run-to-run noise of the log
being off (six alternating rounds at 16 clients: medians 3,735 and 3,886 µs).

---

## MCP changes

- **Cache.** `pagesift mcp http` opens the result cache from `[cache]` (`enabled`, `dir`,
  `max_mb`), as `serve` does. `mcp stdio` still runs without it: each client starts its own
  process.
- **One process per data directory.** The store now takes a lock file. If another process holds
  the directory, `mcp http` prints a warning and runs without the cache; `serve` reports the
  conflict.
- **Warnings in text.** `pagesift_scrape` adds a `Warnings: thin_content, …` line under the
  title and URL. The full warnings stay in the structured result.
- **Shutdown.** On `SIGTERM` the HTTP transport stops accepting requests, then the browser pool
  is closed.
- **Library API.** `pagesift::mcp::run_server` is unchanged; `run_server_until` takes a shutdown
  future.

---

## Upgrade notes

- The minimum supported Rust version is 1.89 (standard-library file locks).
- Running `serve` and `mcp http` against the same data directory is no longer possible at the
  same time: give them different `[cache] dir` values, or let `mcp http` run without the cache.
- No configuration keys were renamed or removed; `[audit]` is new.

name: v0.73.0
body:
# PageSift 0.73.0 Release Notes: All Cores Again, Hardened Inputs, Fewer False Positives

> **Release Version**: `v0.73.0`
> **Release Date**: 2026-10-26
> **License**: AGPL-3.0-only (Commercial licensing available)

---

## Overview

0.73.0 is a fix release driven by a three-way code review (correctness, architecture, release
process) and about 150 adversarial input tests: broken encodings, pathological HTML, malformed
HTTP, redirect and SSRF tricks, hostile feeds, crawl traps and API abuse.

- **Content extraction uses every core again.** Since 0.70.0, `scrape`, `crawl` and `serve`
  extracted pages on a single core. The API server now serves 5–7× more requests per second.
- Crashes, data corruption and denial-of-service paths found by the review are closed.
- Several 0.72.8 heuristics that misfired on real pages are narrowed — for example, short
  Substack posts were reported as age-verification barriers.
- The API server enforces timeouts against slow clients and upper bounds on every parameter.

All numbers below were measured on the same machine (i7-10700, 8 cores / 16 threads, 15 GB),
with 0.72.8 and 0.73.0 run alternately under identical conditions.

---

## Extraction runs on all cores again

`CPU_SLOTS`, the semaphore that bounds concurrent extraction, sized itself with
`std::thread::available_parallelism()`. On Linux that returns the **calling thread's** CPU
affinity. The semaphore is initialized lazily on a tokio worker, and since 0.70.0 the CLI pins
every runtime thread to a single CPU — so the semaphore always had exactly one permit.

0.73.0 sets the capacity from the cgroup-aware hardware topology on the main thread before any
thread is pinned, and pins only the runtime workers; blocking-pool threads (extraction, PDF
parsing) are left to the scheduler.

| `serve`, `/v1/scrape`, 16 concurrent clients | 0.72.8 | 0.73.0 |
| :--- | ---: | ---: |
| Requests per second (higher is better) | 309–336 | 1,153–2,196 |
| p50 latency (lower is better) | 36–45 ms | 4.5–6.1 ms |
| Peak server RSS (lower is better) | 53–56 MB | 89–92 MB |

The higher memory is the cost of running 16 extractions at once instead of one. The figures
above used the `auto` engine, which sends some pages to a browser for 1–7 s each. With
`engine: http` and the default global concurrency of 64, 16/32/64 clients reach 2,373/2,540/
2,458 requests per second — about 88% of what in-process extraction alone achieves on this
machine — so the server itself is not the bottleneck.

**Memory allocator.** The release binary keeps glibc malloc limited to 4 arenas with a 256 KB
mmap threshold (pure Rust, no bundled allocator). On this 16-thread machine that was the fastest
setting tested: 16 arenas, glibc defaults and jemalloc were all slower or used 2–3× the memory.
It has **not** been verified on large multi-socket servers, where a fixed 4 arenas may become a
lock bottleneck; the 0.70.0 figures from a 192-vCPU server were measured with a benchmark runner
built with mimalloc, not with the release binary.

---

## Crashes, corruption and denial of service

| Problem | 0.72.8 | 0.73.0 |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| CJK page whose byte 4096 falls inside a character | panic, `INTERNAL_ERROR` | extracted |
| UTF-8 page with a few stray Latin-1 bytes | whole page re-decoded as Windows-1252 | UTF-8 kept, stray bytes become U+FFFD |
| PDF served as `application/octet-stream` | rejected as binary | parsed as PDF |
| One element with 40,000 attributes | 3.00 s | 0.02 s |
| Client sending one header byte every 5 s | connection held indefinitely | closed after the 30 s header timeout |
| RSS item `<link>javascript:…</link>` | emitted as a Markdown link | dropped |
| Lightpanda + `--allow-cidr`, subresource `[::ffff:127.0.0.1]` | not in the block list | blocked |

---

## Heuristics that misfired on real pages

- **Age gates.** 0.72.8 treated `age-gate`/`age_gate` in the raw HTML as proof of an
  age-verification page when the page had little visible text. Substack pages carry
  `"test_age_gate_user":false` in their inline JSON, and `language-gate` matched too. The rule
  only fired when the marker fell in the scanned part of the HTML and the page showed under
  2,000 characters, so long articles were unaffected: on 66 real Substack pages, 0.72.8 rejected
  2 short "hidden open thread" posts with `ACCESS_BARRIER` and 0.73.0 rejects none. Age gates
  are now recognized from visible confirmation text only. Steam's age check is covered by a
  local test; Steam currently shows no age check to anonymous visitors from our test location,
  so it could not be re-checked live.
- **Author lists** are matched by whole class/id tokens (`authors`, `author-list`,
  `ltx_authors`…) and only exempt from link-density pruning. Sidebar "our writers" widgets and
  footer author boxes are pruned again; arXiv keeps its author line.
- **`v-cloak` / `x-cloak`** on a `<body>` child holding more than 1,000 characters is treated as
  a hydrating app root, not a hidden template.
- **`<template>`** content can no longer be selected as the article body.
- **`excerpt`** is no longer a negative class. `teaser` stays: removing it put product-page
  review previews back into the output (WCXB product −0.009).
- **`openai_key`** requires a real key shape; on 500 real pages it went from 12 false positives
  (CSS variables such as `sk-line-height--extralarge`) to 0.
- **VideoObject fallback** only replaces a body that is essentially empty (under 30 characters).

---

## Protocol handling

- `Content-Encoding: gzip, gzip` is decoded in reverse order, up to three layers, each layer
  bounded by the body size limit.
- A body labelled gzip/zstd without the format's magic bytes is used as-is with a
  `content_encoding_mismatch` warning; a corrupt stream reports a decoding error rather than
  "exceeded the size limit".
- A `Location` header with raw UTF-8 (or Latin-1) bytes is percent-encoded and followed; SSRF
  checks and the redirect limit apply as before.
- `application/json` responses become a formatted ```json code block.
- A final 3xx without a usable `Location` warns `http_redirect_status`; a 304 to an
  unconditional request warns `not_modified`; `pagesift scrape` exits 2 for both when the body
  is empty.
- With a proxy configured, hostnames are resolved locally only when `allow_cidrs`/`allow_ips`
  are set, so `socks5h` users no longer leak DNS. A host resolving inside an allowed range still
  connects directly; a failed lookup (2 s cap) falls back to the proxy.

---

## Crawl scope

Where should a crawl stay when you start it at `https://example.com/blog/post-3`? Earlier
versions picked one fixed rule and were each wrong half the time: 0.70 crawled one page,
0.71–0.72.8 always went up a directory (so `/docs/python` also crawled `/docs/java`). 0.73.0
decides from what the start page links to.

1. Start in the narrowest directory: the seed's own path, or the directory of a file-name seed.
2. After fetching the start page, count its links below that directory (children). If the page
   has body text (≥ 200 letters or digits outside links) and fewer than 3 children, it is a leaf
   page: walk up from the parent directory and widen to the nearest one the page links at least
   3 sibling pages in. Never widen to the site root. Walking up matters for date-based URLs —
   `/2024/Dec/31/post/` has no siblings on the same day but many in `/2024/Dec/`. A trailing
   slash does not make a seed a directory; directory pages are recognized by their children.
3. Say so: `warning: crawl_scope: widened path scope from /blog/post-3/ to /blog/ (…)`.
   Sitemap URLs held back by the narrow scope are queued after widening.

| Seed | 0.70 | 0.71–0.72.8 | 0.73.0 `auto` |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `/docs/python` (has child pages) | `/docs/python/*` | `/docs/*` | `/docs/python/*` |
| `/docs/index.html` | nothing followed | `/docs/*` | `/docs/*` |
| `/blog/post-3` (article, links other posts) | 1 page | `/blog/*` | `/blog/*`, with warning |
| `/shop/c/socks` (empty category, links only) | 1 page | `/shop/c/*` | 1 page |
| `/about` (directly under the root) | 1 page | 1 page | 1 page |

`--scope exact` never widens, `--scope parent` starts in the page's section — the parent
directory, skipping year/month/day directories (`/blog/2026/07/21/post/` → `/blog/`), or the
whole host when that section is the root — and `--scope domain` (or `--entire-domain`) crawls
the host. The API takes the same values in `scope`;
`crawlEntireDomain: true` still means `domain`.

Measured on local test sites (higher is better). The rules were written against the first set;
the two holdout sets were written afterwards with their expected results fixed in advance, and
no threshold was changed after seeing them (only the planned body-text check was added after
holdout 1 found an empty category page widening):

| Set | 0.72.8 precision / recall | 0.73.0 before this change | 0.73.0 |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Development, 7 cases | 0.804 / 1.000 | 1.000 / 0.631 | 1.000 / 1.000 |
| Holdout 1, 5 cases | 0.810 / 0.971 | 1.000 / 0.314 | 1.000 / 0.821 |
| Holdout 2, 4 cases | 0.577 / 1.000 | 1.000 / 0.564 | 1.000 / 1.000 |

On the real web (limit 15 pages, `engine: http`, robots.txt honoured; recall is measured against
a whole-host crawl restricted to the intended section with the same limit). Batch 1 was run
before the ancestor walk was added; batch 2 used sites not seen before, with intended sections
written down before the run:

| Real sites (precision / recall) | 0.72.8 | 0.73.0 before this change | 0.73.0 |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Batch 1: Python, Rust book/std, Go, MDN, React, GitHub Docs, Kubernetes, BBC, three blogs, Substack (14) | 0.983 / 0.863 | 1.000 / 0.547 | 0.983 / 0.929 |
| Batch 2: Django ×2, FastAPI, Docker, Node, PostgreSQL, Fowler, Go blog, Ars Technica, Joel on Software (10) | 0.993 / 0.543 | 1.000 / 0.457 | 0.993 / 0.820 |

Batch 2 excludes LWN, which returned no pages to any version. Pages the start page links to
outside the intended section (precision below 1) are mostly one stray link per crawl, such as
Go's `/doc/` linking `/doc/devel/`.

Known misses, where the start page itself carries no evidence:
- Posts that link only their previous and next post (jvns.ca, joelonsoftware.com) stay narrow.
  `--scope parent` crawls the section (`/blog/`) or, for root-level date URLs, the site.
- News articles whose related links all point to other sections (Ars Technica `/gadgets/…`
  linking `/science/…`) stay narrow; widening to the whole site needs `--entire-domain`.
- When nothing is followed, the `crawl_followed_zero` warning now suggests `--scope parent`.

---

## API limits and error format

| Parameter | Limit |
| :--- | :--- |
| scrape `timeout` | 300,000 ms |
| crawl `limit` | 100,000 |
| crawl `maxDepth` / `maxDiscoveryDepth` | 100 |
| map `limit` | 100,000 |
| URLs per batch scrape / extract | 10,000 |
| URL length | 8 KB |
| request headers / request body | 30 s each |
| whole synchronous request | 360 s |

`extract.schema` must be a JSON object. Query-string and path-parameter errors, 405 and 415 now
return the standard `{"success": false, "code": …, "error": …}` body.

---

## Quality and performance

Extraction quality on three labeled sets (all higher is better):

| Set | Metric | 0.72.8 | 0.73.0 |
| :--- | :--- | ---: | ---: |
| AEB (181 news pages) | F1 | 0.958 | 0.958 |
| Firecrawl (597 pages) | content score | 0.680 | 0.682 |
| WCXB (1,869 pages) | F1 | 0.8522 | 0.8533 |
| WCXB listing | F1 | 0.6925 | 0.7065 |
| WCXB product | F1 | 0.6467 | 0.6467 |

Page-by-page across all 2,647 pages: no crashes, no page emptied, two pages shrank by more than
30% (one lost a run of decorative asterisks; one tag page lost its heading together with its
boilerplate).

Speed, alternating old/new runs (lower is better):

| Benchmark | 0.72.8 | 0.73.0 | Change |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Extraction, 2,786 real pages, 1 thread | 6.405 s | 6.198 s | −3.2% |
| Extraction, 2,786 real pages, 16 threads | 1.034 s | 0.979 s | −5.3% |
| Synthetic blog page 100 KB (`perf_gate`) | 3.73 ms | 3.78 ms | +1.3% |
| Synthetic wiki page 250 KB (`perf_gate`) | 16.31 ms | 16.61 ms | +1.8% |
| Charset detection, 3,192 files | 2.043 s | 2.004 s | −1.9% |
| `crawl` 1,000 pages, one host | 1.96–2.02 s | 1.95–2.00 s | ±0 |

Binary size: 38,478,112 → 38,657,584 bytes (+0.47%).

---

## Re-checked on the live web

Each fix that has a public example was re-run against real sites with 0.72.8 and 0.73.0
(`engine: http`, robots.txt honoured):

| Check | 0.72.8 | 0.73.0 |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| PDF served by raw.githubusercontent.com as `application/octet-stream` | refused (`UNSUPPORTED_OPTION`) | 94,696 characters |
| `api.github.com` JSON | plain text | ```json code block |
| `httpbin.org/status/304` | exit 0, empty, no warning | exit 2, `not_modified` |
| `httpbin.org/status/300` (no `Location`) | exit 0, `empty_content` | exit 2, `http_redirect_status` |
| 66 Substack pages | 2 rejected as age gates | 0 |
| jvns.ca Atom feed with `[DEST]` in code | unescaped brackets | `\[DEST\]` |
| Chinese Atom feed, GBK and Shift_JIS pages, arXiv authors, YouTube | correct | identical |

A broader pass over 45 real pages (news, docs, shops, forums, Chinese/Japanese/Korean portals,
feeds, a PDF) changed nothing except the fixes above, plus one Wikipedia paragraph with a code
sample that 0.72.8 dropped and 0.73.0 keeps. Six pages fail identically in both versions, all
correctly reported: four disallow crawlers in robots.txt, two sit behind DataDome or Cloudflare
challenges.

The single-core fix does not show in polite crawls of real sites: crawling 150 Rust `std` pages
takes about 1.1 s in both versions and uses about 1.2 s of CPU, so the network is the limit. It
matters when extraction is the bottleneck, as in a `serve` instance under concurrent load.

---

## Upgrade notes

- Crawls from a directory-like seed with its own child pages (`/docs/python`) no longer reach
  sibling directories as in 0.71–0.72.8; use `--scope parent`, `--entire-domain` or `--include`.
- Proxy users who reach intranet hostnames directly should list them in `NO_PROXY` or keep
  `--allow-cidr` set so they are resolved locally.
- Scripts checking `pagesift scrape`'s exit code now see 2 for empty 3xx/304 results.
- API clients sending values above the new limits receive HTTP 400 with the limit in the message.

name: v0.72.8
body:
# PageSift 0.72.8 Release Notes: Truthful Signals, Complete Allow-Lists, Better Extraction

> **Release Version**: `v0.72.8`
> **Release Date**: 2026-10-26
> **License**: AGPL-3.0-only (Commercial licensing available)

---

## Overview

0.72.8 closes the fourth-round audit (charset, allow-lists, config, exit codes) and the
fifth-to-eighth-round field audit (extraction quality, metadata fidelity and honest signals).

- HTTP charset headers that lie no longer produce silent mojibake.
- `--allow-cidr` covers every command that fetches, not only `scrape`.
- `crawl` and `map` no longer report a failed seed as a successful empty result.
- `pagesift` loads the platform config file by default, and `doctor` shows which file it read.
- Recipe pages keep their ingredients, GitHub code pages keep their code, arXiv pages keep
  their authors, RSS feeds become item lists, and thin or barrier pages say so.

---

## Charset headers are verified against the body

`Content-Type` and `<meta>` charset declarations are treated as candidates instead of facts.
After decoding, Pagesift checks whether the declaration actually fits the bytes:

- **UTF-8 declared, GBK body** — the declared decode produces replacement characters; Pagesift
  re-detects the body and decodes it as GBK.
- **Latin-1/Windows-1252 declared, UTF-8 body** — the declared decode succeeds byte-wise but is
  mojibake; Pagesift recognizes the valid UTF-8 body and decodes it as UTF-8.
- **Small local damage** — one or two bad bytes do not switch the whole page; the text is kept
  and a warning is emitted.

Every correction is visible in `metadata.pagesift.warnings`, for example:

```text
decode: Content-Type declared UTF-8 but decoding produced 70 replacement characters; decoded as GBK instead
decode: Content-Type declared windows-1252 but the body is valid UTF-8; decoded as UTF-8 instead
```

Correctly declared UTF-8, GBK, Shift_JIS, Big5, EUC-KR and Windows-1252 pages are unchanged.
The UTF-8 fast path remains allocation-free. Encoding names in warnings use the WHATWG
canonical name, so a header saying `iso-8859-1` is reported as `windows-1252`.

---

## `--allow-cidr` everywhere

The same private-network allow-list is now available on:

```text
scrape  crawl  map  download  session-fetch  collect  serve
```

- Applies to HTTP fetching and browser rendering.
- Repeatable: `--allow-cidr 10.0.0.0/8 --allow-cidr 198.18.0.0/15`.
- Invalid values fail during argument parsing (`rc=2`) instead of being silently dropped:

```text
error: invalid value 'not-a-cidr' for '--allow-cidr <CIDR>': invalid CIDR "not-a-cidr"
```

`mcp` has no URL command-line surface and continues to read `fetch.allow_cidrs` from the config
file.

---

## Honest crawl and map failures

- `map` previously returned exit code 0 and printed only the seed URL when the seed fetch failed.
  It now returns the original error (`SSRF_BLOCKED`, timeout, DNS failure, ...) with empty stdout.
- `crawl` now exits with code 1 when it collected **zero pages and at least one error**. Partial
  success still exits 0, preserving the existing contract for large crawls.
- `crawl` no longer sends a short static page through the browser a second time just because the
  text is short. Auto-rendering now requires client code or a substantial HTML document, so the
  seed page is fetched once in the common static case.

---

## Default configuration discovery

Lookup order:

```text
--config  >  PAGESIFT_CONFIG  >  platform config file (only if it exists)  >  built-in defaults
```

Platform paths:

| Platform | Path |
| :--- | :--- |
| Linux / macOS | `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/pagesift/pagesift.toml`, else `$HOME/.config/pagesift/pagesift.toml` |
| Windows | `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/pagesift/pagesift.toml`, else `%APPDATA%\pagesift\pagesift.toml`, else `%USERPROFILE%\.config\pagesift\pagesift.toml` |

`XDG_CONFIG_HOME` must be an absolute path. Empty and relative values are treated as unset, so a
broken environment cannot make Pagesift read `./.config/...` from the current directory.

`PAGESIFT_CONFIG=` (empty value) disables all config files — useful for Docker, CI and tests:

```bash
PAGESIFT_CONFIG= pagesift doctor   # built-in defaults only
```

`doctor` now reports the real source:

```text
ok   config: /home/me/.config/pagesift/pagesift.toml
ok   config: defaults (no config file; create /home/me/.config/pagesift/pagesift.toml to add one)
ok   config: defaults (config files disabled by PAGESIFT_CONFIG=)
```

### Upgrade note

If a `pagesift.toml` already exists in the platform config directory, commands that previously
used built-in defaults will now load it. Run `pagesift doctor` after upgrading to confirm the
source. Use `--config`, `PAGESIFT_CONFIG` or `PAGESIFT_CONFIG=` to override discovery explicitly.

Thanks to **@w21180239** for proposing default config discovery in PR #3.

---

## Extraction quality and honest signals

### Recipe and content asides are kept

Body selection no longer throws away an `<aside>` that belongs to the article. Content asides
inside `<main>`/`<article>` are kept when they are not named like a sidebar and do not consist
mostly of links. Recipe ingredient lists are the common case: the King Arthur chocolate-chip
cookie page now returns the title, all ingredients and the full method instead of a 468-character
introduction.

A preview block (`quickview`, `teaser`, `excerpt`) is no longer mistaken for the article itself.

### GitHub code pages keep the code

GitHub's file view renders line numbers and code as two sibling columns. Pagesift now:

- drops the `react-line-numbers` column;
- merges the `react-file-line` rows into one fenced code block, in order;
- skips visually-hidden headings such as "Repository navigation".

A 411-line Rust file used to produce 411 standalone numeric lines and an unfenced code blob; it
now produces one code fence and no numeric noise.

### Authors and citation metadata

- Author blocks (`authors`, `author-list`) survive link-density pruning, so arXiv abstract pages
  keep the author line in the body.
- `citation_author`, `citation_title`, `citation_doi`, `citation_journal_title`,
  `citation_conference_title`, `citation_pdf_url` and `citation_arxiv_id` are read from `<meta>`.
  Multiple `citation_author` values are joined with commas into `metadata.author`.
- `metadata.pagesift.jsonLd` now carries every parsed JSON-LD block unchanged, so downstream
  pipelines can consume `Article`, `Recipe`, `Product` and `VideoObject` data directly.

### Barriers and interstitials

Generic German, French and Spanish block pages are classified as `ACCESS_BARRIER` instead of
being delivered as content (the ZEIT 403 page is the reference case). Age-verification pages are
reported with a new `interstitial` barrier kind. Known vendor rules are unchanged; this only
fills gaps for sites without a vendor signature.

### Thin extraction has a signal

When a 2xx page has a substantial HTML document but less than 500 non-whitespace characters of
extracted text, Pagesift adds:

```text
thin_content: extracted 468 characters from 331 KB of HTML; the page may be a JavaScript shell or the main content was not selected
```

This distinguishes "the page is genuinely small" from "the content was dropped". `empty_content`
still covers literal zero.

### `inspect` recognizes more secrets

New `secret_indicator` rules cover:

- OpenAI-style keys (`sk-…`, `sk-proj-…`, `sk-ant-…`);
- JWTs (three base64url segments);
- `api_key = "…"` / `api-key: "…"` assignments.

GitHub tokens, AWS keys, Stripe keys, Slack tokens and private keys were already covered. Values
are still never echoed; findings only contain rule names and byte offsets.

### Images keep their `title`

Markdown images now include the `title` attribute, which is where some sites put the caption:
`![Standards](https://imgs.xkcd.com/comics/standards.png "Fortunately, the charging one …")`.
Alt text behaviour is unchanged.

### RSS, Atom and RDF feeds are parsed, not scraped

Feeds are detected by structure and converted to a Markdown item list:

```markdown
# xkcd.com

xkcd.com: A webcomic of romance and math humor.

- [Forms of Water](https://xkcd.com/3315/) — Fri, 23 Oct 2026 04:00:00 -0000
```

Escaped HTML in descriptions is stripped and entities are restored. `--only-links` returns the
item links. Sitemaps are still handled by the crawl/map path, not by this parser.

### Video pages use their embedded metadata

When a video page has no readable body text, the page's JSON-LD `VideoObject` supplies the
title, description, author and upload date. The result carries an honest warning:

```text
video_metadata: no readable body text; used the page's embedded video metadata
```

YouTube watch pages now return the video title and description on the HTTP path instead of an
empty document and a bare `empty_content` warning.

### Smaller fixes

- `pagesift diagnose` prints the actual version instead of the hard-coded `0.60`.

---

## Verification

At the time of writing:

```text
cargo test --workspace                     784 passed, 0 failed
```

Field probes on the 0.72.8 binary:

| Case | Before | After |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| King Arthur recipe | 468 chars, no ingredients | 2,693 chars, 6 `teaspoon`, title + ingredients + method |
| GitHub `core/src/lib.rs` | 1,589 lines, 411 numeric lines, no fence | 425 lines, 0 numeric lines, one fenced block |
| arXiv `1706.03762` | `Vaswani` absent, `author: null` | author line in body, 8 authors in metadata |
| ZEIT 403 block page | success + `http_error_status` | `ACCESS_BARRIER` (`generic.denied_de`) |
| xkcd RSS | escaped soup | clean item list |
| xkcd #927 image | no title | `title` preserved |
| YouTube watch page | 0 chars + `empty_content` | title + description + `video_metadata` |
| `inspect` fixture | AWS only | AWS, OpenAI key, JWT, api_key assignment |
| `diagnose` | `PageSift 0.60` | `PageSift 0.72.8` |
| crawl seed (auto engine) | 2 requests | 1 request |

Correctly declared legacy charsets, 4.49 MB pages, PDFs, tables, browser rendering and normal
crawls are unchanged.

---

## Known boundaries

- A certificate used as both CA and leaf (`CaUsedAsEndEntity`) is classified as `other TLS
  error`; the common expired / hostname-mismatch / untrusted-root cases have distinct codes.
- `map --sitemap only` still returns only the seed URL if the sitemap itself fails; that mode
  intentionally skips the seed scrape.
- `mcp` remains config-file only.
- Framework-rendered visible text and server-side i18n are unchanged; the video fallback relies
  on page-declared JSON-LD and does not execute JavaScript.
- A page that is thin because it really is a short note can still receive `thin_content`; it is
  a warning, not an error, and never changes the extracted text.

---

## Docker

```bash
docker pull ghcr.io/yolow92/pagesift:0.72.8
```

# PageSift 0.71.0 Release Notes: Honest Failure Reporting and Safer Crawling

> **Release Version**: `v0.71.0`
> **Release Date**: 2026-10-26
> **License**: AGPL-3.0-only (Commercial licensing available)

---

## Overview

0.71.0 is a bug-fix release for issues found in the 0.70.0 field audit. It does not change the
extraction engine or the public response contract. The focus is on making failures visible and
making authorization apply consistently:

- crawls that start from a file URL now cover the whole site;
- local files and network responses use the same charset logic;
- `NO_PROXY` and `--allow-cidr` are honored on every path;
- binary, empty and captcha responses are no longer reported as ordinary success;
- TLS certificate failures have their own machine-readable error codes;
- browser authorization matches HTTP authorization;
- root/sandbox and auto-fallback failures explain themselves;
- CLI exit codes distinguish a failed request from an HTTP error page;
- framework-hidden templates no longer leak into Markdown;
- piping CLI output into `head` or another early-closing reader no longer panics.

All ten audit items are fixed and covered by regression tests. Performance is unchanged within
measurement noise; peak RSS grew by 1.6–4.1% (below the 5% release gate).

---

## Fixes

### Crawl scope

`crawl https://example.com/index.html` now scopes the crawl to the containing directory instead
of treating `index.html/` as the prefix. A seed whose links are all filtered emits a
`crawl_followed_zero` warning instead of silently returning one page.

### Charset handling

`convert` now uses the same BOM → meta prescan → detection pipeline as network fetching, and
accepts `--charset` for explicit overrides. BOM, `meta charset`, legacy `http-equiv`, Shift_JIS,
EUC-JP, GBK, Big5, windows-1251 and KOI8-R are covered.

### Proxy and allow-list semantics

`NO_PROXY` / `no_proxy` are honored for environment proxies. Targets admitted by
`--allow-cidr`, `allow_hosts` or `allow_ips` connect directly. Named egress proxies still keep
their explicit proxy semantics and are not bypassed by allow-lists.

### Honest content reporting

- Image, audio, video, font and archive responses return `UNSUPPORTED_OPTION` instead of being
  decoded as text. HTML mislabeled as `application/octet-stream` is still accepted.
- HTTP < 400 responses with no extractable text carry an `empty_content` warning.
- bilibili captcha pages return `ACCESS_BARRIER` with vendor `bilibili`.

### Browser authorization

Browser sub-requests consume the same `allow_hosts` / `allow_ips` / `allow_cidrs` list as HTTP
fetching. Chrome uses the CDP allow-list guard; Lightpanda receives matching `--block-cidrs`
exemptions. A browser request without an allow-list is still blocked from private networks.

### TLS classification

Certificate failures are no longer folded into `NETWORK_ERROR`:

| Error code | Meaning |
| :--- | :--- |
| `TLS_CERT_EXPIRED` | certificate expired or not yet valid |
| `TLS_HOSTNAME_MISMATCH` | certificate does not cover the requested host |
| `TLS_UNTRUSTED_ROOT` | chain not trusted (self-signed, missing issuer) |
| `TLS_ERROR` | other TLS handshake/certificate error |

Classification works on direct connections, CONNECT proxies, reqwest-based proxied transfers and
Chrome navigation errors (`ERR_CERT_*`). Certificate failures are deterministic failures and do
not enter network-jitter backoff.

### Root diagnostics and auto fallback

`pagesift doctor` reports the browser as `FAIL` when running as root and explains the Chrome
sandbox constraint. `scrape --engine browser` reports the launch failure reason instead of
"no browser engine found". `--engine auto` prints the downgrade reason in CLI Markdown mode and
keeps `render_unavailable` in `metadata.pagesift.warnings`.

### CLI exit codes

| Situation | Exit code | Warning |
| :--- | ---: | :--- |
| HTTP < 500 with content | 0 | — |
| HTTP 404 with empty content | 2 | `http_error_status: HTTP 404` |
| HTTP >= 500 | 2 | `http_error_status: HTTP 500` |
| robots/barrier/network/request failure | 1 | error code |

The JSON body keeps `success=true` for fetched error pages so the Firecrawl-compatible contract
is unchanged; the CLI exit code and warning make the page status visible to scripts.

### Hidden templates

Elements marked `x-cloak`, `data-cloak`, `v-cloak` or `ng-cloak` are treated as pre-hydration
templates and filtered. App shells containing `main`, `article` or `role=main` are preserved.
Plain `display:none`, `hidden`, `template` and `aria-hidden` behavior is unchanged.

### CLI pipes

`pagesift doctor | head -1` and similar pipelines now exit with the conventional SIGPIPE status
141 instead of printing a Rust panic and exiting 101. Stdout and stderr writes detect
`BrokenPipe` and stop quietly; the network stack is unchanged.

---

## Verification

- `cargo test --workspace`: 748 passed, 0 failed.
- Node binding: 38/38 including the event-loop responsiveness suite.
- `step2/verify_p0.sh`: 16/16.
- `step3/verify_p1.sh`: 12/12.
- `step4/verify_p2.sh`: 13/13.
- `step5/regression.sh`: 20/20, including tables, a 4.5 MB Markdown page, PDF, legacy charsets,
  browser rendering, crawl seeds and redirect semantics.
- Performance: no timing regression; RSS +1.6–4.1% in same-condition old/new comparisons.

---

## Known limits

- moli does not accept negative CIDR exemptions; fine-grained `--allow-cidr` still cannot pass
  its kernel-level `--block-private-networks` guard. Chrome and Lightpanda are covered.
- Browser DNS rebinding remains the same risk as the existing `PrivateNetworkGuard`; CIDR checks
  use the local resolution result.
- Only framework/CSS-hidden templates are filtered. Visible server-rendered i18n text remains
  page content and is not removed heuristically.

---

## Upgrade

No configuration or API changes are required.

```bash
docker pull ghcr.io/yolow92/pagesift:0.71.0
```

CLI scripts that treat any non-zero exit code as failure should account for exit code 2
("page fetched, HTTP status is an error") if they intentionally fetch 404/5xx pages.

body:
# PageSift 0.70.0 Release Notes: The NUMA Data-Plane Rewrite

> **Release Version**: `v0.70.0`
> **License**: AGPL-3.0-only (Commercial licensing available)
> **Core Architecture**: Pure Safe Rust (`#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`), hand-written NUMA-local HTTP/1.1 data plane, adaptive closed-loop capacity control

---

## 🌟 Executive Overview

0.60 proved PageSift could finish 100,000,000 tasks. 0.70 replaces the engine underneath that result:
the generic async-HTTP stack is gone, replaced by a **purpose-built, NUMA-local Rust data plane**,
and the whole system is now governed by one closed-loop controller that senses hardware, memory
cgroups and per-origin behaviour instead of trusting fixed constants.

Three outcomes define this release:

1. **Scaling is now measured, not assumed** — 1 → 192 vCPU in one ladder, fitted with the Universal
   Scalability Law.
2. **Memory became a first-class input** — the engine reads its cgroup limit and sizes itself to it.
3. **Extraction quality is reported against public benchmarks** — seven independent suites, published
   number-by-number, including the ones we do not win.

---

## 🚀 Key Highlights

### 1. ⚙️ Hand-Written NUMA-Local HTTP Data Plane

The 0.60 data path funnelled every request through a general-purpose client. 0.70 builds the path
from the socket up, in five layers:

| Layer | What it does |
| :--- | :--- |
| **NUMA-local fixed-slot executor** | Content workers are pinned; each slot owns its buffers for the life of the process |
| **NUMA-local HTTP/1.1 reactor** | Minimal request/response state machine, zero per-request allocation for headers |
| **Hybrid reactor scheduling** | Reactor and content threads share one pipeline; work budget moves between them at runtime |
| **Adaptive per-host connections** | Connection watermarks are per-origin, measured, and closed-loop — a slow host no longer drags the rest |
| **NUMA-native dispatch + work stealing** | Sharded intake with bounded stealing; empty polls are cheap, starvation is visible in telemetry |

Fused parse pipeline: bytes land in the NUMA node that owns the connection, are parsed there, and the
Markdown is produced without a cross-node copy.

### 2. 📈 Scaling Measured 1 → 192 vCPU, Fitted with USL

One ladder, same binary, same fixtures, from a single core to the full 192 vCPU dual-Xeon box:

```
QPS(N) = γ·N / (1 + σ·(N−1) + κ·N·(N−1))
```

| Parameter | Value | Reading |
| :--- | ---: | :--- |
| γ (per-core ceiling) | **8,631.8 pages/s** | single-core ceiling |
| σ (contention) | **1.3407 %** | near-linear; little serialisation |
| κ (coherency) | **0.0000 %** | **no measurable cross-core penalty** |
| R² | 0.8388 | fit quality across the ladder |

κ = 0 is the headline: the data plane does not pay a coherency tax as cores are added, because
nothing is shared on the hot path.

### 3. 🧠 Memory Becomes an Input, Not an Assumption

`HardwareTopology::read_memory()` now reads cgroup v2 `memory.max` and pushes the cap into the
capacity controller. Measured under hard limits:

| cgroup limit | Concurrency | Result |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **768 MiB** | 380 | 50M/50M, 0 failures, **817,346 p/s**, RSS 730 MiB |
| 1 GiB | 1,536 | 50M/50M, 0 failures, 1,063,283 p/s |
| 2 GiB | 1,536 | 50M/50M, 0 failures, 1,068,726 p/s |

At 768 MiB the controller voluntarily shrinks to 380 connections instead of collapsing to the
minimum — memory pressure turns into lower concurrency, not into OOM.

### 4. 🏁 200M Saturation on 192 vCPU

| Metric | Value |
| :--- | ---: |
| Tasks | **200,000,000 / 200,000,000** |
| Failures | **0** |
| Sustained throughput | **947,611 pages/s** |
| Wall clock | **211.057 s** |
| Peak RSS | **888.1 MiB** (gate: < 2 GiB) |
| Average cores used | **150.0 / 192** |
| Samples verified | 20,000 (1/10,000), all unique |

Against the 0.61 baseline on the same box (`427,033.53 pages/s` at 43.8 % CPU, 84.1 cores), that is
**2.22× absolute** and **+24.4 % per core** (6,317 vs 5,078 pages/s/core), with memory still under
1 GiB and CPU per page down from 196.9 µs to 158.3 µs.

The same binary on a 16-core development box reproduces **6,015 pages/s/core** — within 4.8 % of the
192-core run — so the scaling is the data plane's, not the machine's.

### 5. 📊 Seven-Domain Public Showdown, Including the Losses

Every number below is a full-set run on **one machine**, with the suite's own scorer, under a
**10 GiB memory cap** shared by PageSift and every competitor. Where we lose, the loss is printed.

Measured on Intel i7-10700 (8C/16T), 15 GB RAM, Ubuntu 26.04.

| # | Domain | PageSift 0.70 | Best competitor | Rank |
| :---: | :--- | :--- | :--- | :---: |
| **D1** | Content extraction (WCXB 2,006) | 0.6720 F1 | 0.6824 (PageSift 0.50) | 4th |
| **D3** | PDF extraction (1,403 PDFs / 7,019 checks) | **0.4506** | 0.2446 (pymupdf4llm) | **1st** |
| **D5** | RAG chunking + BM25 (472 questions) | **0.9470** R@5 | 0.9364 (semchunk) | **1st** |
| **D6** | Charset detection (3,128 files) | **0.7602** | 0.7113 (chardet) | **1st** |
| **D7** | Structured data (2,006 pages) | **0.7392** | 0.5488 (bs4+lxml) | **1st** |
| **D9** | Dynamic rendering (7 SPA scenarios) | 3/7 | 5/7 (Playwright) | 2nd |
| **D4** | DOM self-healing (2,000 mutations) | 0.8215 | 0.8875 (Scrapling) | 2nd |

**Four of seven won.** Speed where it matters: 1,403 PDFs in **0.83 s** (31× faster than pypdf,
296× faster than pymupdf4llm); 3,128 encoding detections at **11,239 files/s**; **21 MiB peak** for
structured data. Nothing came close to the 10 GiB cap — the largest competitor peaked at 1,776 MiB,
PageSift at 751 MiB.

The three we did not win, stated plainly:

- **D1** — 0.8854 precision, highest of all 17 entrants, but 0.5989 recall. WCXB's reference text
  includes boilerplate, so whole-page output scores better on this particular metric. We chose
  precision.
- **D9** — client-side and hydration SPAs render correctly, and we finish in **0.47 s vs Playwright's
  2.55 s**. We miss `setTimeout`-delayed injections because we stop at network-idle instead of
  waiting a fixed duration.
- **D4** — we beat Scrapling on adversarial decoys (100 % vs 86.4 %); the overall gap comes from a
  category where **14.6 % of the dataset's labels are wrong** (a `.price` slot contains a person's
  name).

Separately, the seven **standard** suites run earlier remain in the record:
[baselines 1–4](https://github.com/YOLOW92/pagesift/blob/v0.70.0/docs/releases/benchmarks/0.70_p4_step4_2_baselines_1_4.md),
[baselines 5–7](https://github.com/YOLOW92/pagesift/blob/v0.70.0/docs/releases/benchmarks/0.70_p4_step4_2_baselines_5_7.md), and the
[E1 stress suite](https://github.com/YOLOW92/pagesift/blob/v0.70.0/docs/releases/benchmarks/0.70_p4_step4_2_e1.md).

### 6. 🔧 Reliability Fixes Found by the Stress Suite

The E1 stress suite (content storm, multi-host crawl, fault storm, mixed 10-minute run) surfaced
four defects that would have hit production before they hit a benchmark:

| Defect | Fix |
| :--- | :--- |
| `fetch.timeout_secs` did not bound the wait for response headers (8 s configured → 30 s observed) | Budget now propagates to `first_byte_timeout`/`body_idle_timeout`; adaptive tuning no longer overwrites an explicit value |
| A 429 permanently widened the host's request interval (30 s cap, 1/16 decay — effectively unrecoverable) | Halve on success; honour `Retry-After` without permanently penalising the host |
| One permanently-broken URL could freeze an entire host (10 s → 600 s cooldown, unclearable) | Host-level cooldown now counts **distinct** failing URLs, with a flat cooldown |
| Runtime panicked when worker threads could not spawn under a tight `ulimit -v` | Worker count derived from available address space, halving retry, clear error |

After the fixes, the same fault-storm run converges naturally on all four hosts instead of hitting
the 480 s deadline.

### 7. ⚖️ 2.22× Over 0.61, With Less CPU Per Page

| Run | Tasks | Wall | Sustained | Cores used | Per-core | Per-page CPU | Peak RSS |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 0.61 baseline (192 vCPU) | 100M | 234.2 s | 427,033 p/s | 84.1 / 192 | 5,078 | 196.9 µs | — |
| **0.70** (192 vCPU) | **200M** | **211.1 s** | **947,611 p/s** | 150.0 / 192 | **6,317** | **158.3 µs** | 888.1 MiB |
| **0.70** (16 vCPU dev box) | 100M | 1,686.1 s | 59,309 p/s | 9.86 / 16 | **6,015** | **166.2 µs** | 124.1 MiB |

**2.22× absolute throughput, +24.4 % per core, −19.6 % CPU per page.**

Per-core output on a 16-core laptop-class box (6,015 p/s/core) lands within 4.8 % of the 192-core
run (6,317 p/s/core) — the scaling is the data plane's, not a property of one machine.

0.70 also runs article-body location on every page instead of only `og:type=article` pages, which is
worth **+0.055 ROUGE-5 F1** on WebMainBench (0.5860 → 0.6414). Even with that extra work the
per-page CPU stays below 0.61: the data plane saves more than the extraction spends. Set
`PAGESIFT_NO_FORCE_ARTICLE=1` to drop the extra location pass entirely.

---

## 🛠️ Reproducing the 0.70 Numbers

```bash
# 1. 200M local saturation
cd bench/p0 && cargo build --release --bin p2_http_reactor_runner --bin stream_origin
bash bench/p3/run_200m_check.sh <tag>

# 2. Memory envelope (cgroup v2)
systemd-run --user --scope -p MemoryMax=768M \
  ./bench/p0/target/release/p2_http_reactor_runner \
  --formal --mode full --split-pipeline --total-tasks 50000000 --output /tmp/mem768.json

# 3. Seven standard benchmarks + E1
bash bench/scripts/e1a_sweep.sh          # content storm
bash bench/scripts/e1b_crawl.sh          # multi-host crawl
bash bench/scripts/e1c5.sh               # fault storm
bash bench/scripts/e1d_run.sh            # 10-minute mixed

# 4. Quality suites
bench/upstream/.venv/bin/python bench/p4_2_webmainbench/wceb_run.py ...
```

Full reports: [`docs/benchmarks/`](https://github.com/YOLOW92/pagesift/blob/v0.70.0/docs/benchmarks) — every table above links back to a document
with the exact binaries, commit hashes, dataset checksums and scorer versions.

---

## 📦 Upgrade Notes

- **No API breakage.** Rust, Python, Node.js, CLI and the Firecrawl v1/v2 + Jina Reader compatible
  HTTP surface keep their shapes.
- **New config keys**: none required. `[fetch] timeout_secs` now behaves as a true per-request
  budget; if you previously relied on it being ignored for slow origins, raise it explicitly.
- **New escape hatch**: `PAGESIFT_NO_FORCE_ARTICLE=1` restores pre-0.70 extraction scope.
- **Behaviour change**: adaptive tuning no longer overrides explicitly configured timeouts.

---

## 🙏 Thanks

Every benchmark in this release ran on hardware we could rent for a few hours. The numbers are
reproducible because the harnesses, the scorers and the exact commits are in the repository —
including the ones where we lose.

body:
# PageSift 0.61.0 Release Notes

> **Release Version**: `v0.61.0`  
> **Release Date**: October 24, 2026  
> **License**: AGPL-3.0-only (Commercial licensing available)

PageSift 0.61.0 makes same-host batch behavior observable and configurable. It separates admission-queue time from network-fetch time, explains meaningful per-host delays in warnings, and exposes the relevant rate controls through Python's top-level `scrape_many` helper.

## Queue diagnostics

Every scrape now records `metadata.pagesift.timings.queue` in milliseconds. This value covers waiting for global and per-host concurrency slots plus the effective minimum interval between request starts; `metadata.pagesift.timings.fetch` remains the network fetch duration.

When queue time is at least 10 ms, PageSift adds a warning. If `robots.txt` supplied `Crawl-delay`, the warning identifies that policy and reports the effective interval. The same diagnostics are retained for direct browser rendering and HTTP 304 responses.

## Python batch controls

The synchronous top-level helper accepts three new optional keyword arguments:

```python
from pagesift import scrape_many

docs = scrape_many(
    urls,
    concurrency=16,
    max_concurrency=64,
    per_host_concurrency=4,
    request_interval=0.25,
)
```

- `concurrency` controls how many tasks this batch keeps in flight.
- `max_concurrency` controls the scraper's global admission limit.
- `per_host_concurrency` controls simultaneous requests to one host.
- `request_interval` controls the default spacing between request starts; a site-provided `Crawl-delay` still takes precedence.

When any of the three scraper-level controls is supplied, the helper creates a temporary scraper for that batch and closes it afterward. Calls without them continue to use the shared default scraper.

## Auto-render admission fix

An HTTP request upgraded by `engine=auto` previously retained its HTTP admission permit while waiting for a second browser-render admission. A same-host batch could therefore occupy every per-host slot with tasks that were all waiting for another slot. PageSift now releases the HTTP permit before acquiring the browser-render permit, removing that deadlock path.

The default engine remains `auto` for compatibility. In environments without an available browser, callers that know rendering is unnecessary can explicitly choose the HTTP engine and avoid render eligibility checks.

## Compatibility

This release adds optional parameters and metadata without removing existing APIs. Rust workspace crates, `@pagesift/node`, and the dynamically versioned Python package share version `0.61.0`.

# PageSift 0.60.0 Release Notes: The 100-Million Generational Leap > **Release Version**: `v0.60.0` > **Release Date**: October 24, 2026 > **License**: AGPL-3.0-only (Commercial licensing available) > **Core Architecture**: Pure Safe Rust (`#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`), Share-Nothing Multi-Shard Scheduling, Zero-Disk Retention Streaming, 128 GB Memory Defense Envelope

High-Performance, Memory-Bounded Web Content Engine for AI Agents & LLM Pipelines

--- ## 🌟 Executive Overview: What's New in 0.60.0 PageSift 0.60.0 represents a generational milestone in the project's evolution. While 0.50.0 established web-scale feasibility, 0.60.0 shatters the multi-core scaling ceiling and conquers the holy grail of web extraction: **the authentic 100,000,000 (1 亿级) real-world public web showdown**. ### 🚀 Key Highlights 1. **⚡ Share-Nothing Multi-Shard Architecture (`sharded_runner`)**: - **The Single-Thread Dispatch Breakthrough**: In 0.50, single-thread task dispatch reached a physical wall at ~166,666 ops/sec, leaving 80-core servers with 56% idle CPU. Version 0.60 introduces a **Share-Nothing partitioned scheduler** ($S(N) = \lceil N/8 \rceil$), giving each shard its own private semaphore, connection pool, and `#[repr(align(64))]` cache-line-isolated atomic metrics. - **431,412.37 pages/sec on 80 vCPUs AMD EPYC**: Tested end-to-end on Google Cloud `n4d-highcpu-80`, completing 100,000,000 tasks in **231.80 seconds (3.86 minutes)** vs 0.50's 660.14 seconds (11.00 minutes) — **a 2.85× speedup, saving 7.14 minutes per 100M run while elevating CPU utilization from 44% to 83.2%**. - **Linear Multi-Core Scaling**: Eliminates Amdahl's Law contention across 2C~80C. Establishes the continuous autonomous topology formula $C^*(N) = N \times 25$, ready for 300-core and 384-core supernodes with zero performance regression. 2. **💿 Zero-Disk Retention Streaming Pipeline (流式零落盘)**: - **The 2.5 TB Disk Trap Solved**: Crawling 100,000,000 web pages traditionally requires 2~5 TB of disk storage, instantly causing out-of-disk crashes on cloud nodes with 96 GB NVMe SSDs. - **Stream-First Processing**: 16KB constant per-socket memory read buffer $\to$ pure Rust in-memory SIMD decompression (Zstd/Brotli/Gzip) $\to$ semantic Markdown distillation $\to$ Blake3 fingerprint verification $\to$ **immediate deallocation (`drop`) of raw HTML**. - **Result**: The entire 100,000,000 public web crawl increased physical NVMe disk usage by **less than 100 MB**, maintaining over 85 GB of free SSD space throughout the battle. 3. **🛡️ 128 GB Physical Memory Defense Envelope**: - Replaced legacy 12 GB limit with an explicit **128 GB physical defense container envelope (`RLIMIT_AS = 128 GiB`)**, matching modern enterprise production servers. - Maintained a rock-solid steady-state peak RSS of **11.59 GB** (< 8.8% of the 128 GB limit) over 100,000,000 real public web pages with **zero OOM, zero crashes, and zero memory leaks**. 4. **🌐 RFC 7230 Resilient Networking & Anti-WAF Overhaul**: - **RFC 7230 Stale Connection Recovery**: Implemented transparent # PageSift 0.51.0 Release Notes: Network Egress, Granular SSRF Whitelisting, Pip MCP Distribution & Precision Content Cleaning
> **Release Version**: `v0.51.0`  
> **Release Date**: October 24, 2026  
> **License**: AGPL-3.0-only (Commercial licensing available)  
> **Core Architecture**: Pure Safe Rust (`#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`), Zero-Copy Markdown Stream, Zero-Dependency Network Subnetting

---

## 🌟 Executive Overview: What's New in 0.51.0

Following the web-scale milestone of 0.50.0, PageSift 0.51.0 directly addresses real-world industrial testing feedback across containerized environments, proxy networks, academic preprint platforms, and incremental crawling pipelines.

### 🚀 Key Highlights

1. **🌐 Full Proxy & Fake-IP / Remote-DNS Egress Support**:
   - Automatically detects and honors standard system proxy environment variables (`HTTPS_PROXY`, `https_proxy`, `ALL_PROXY`, `all_proxy`, `HTTP_PROXY`, `http_proxy`).
   - CLI adds `--proxy <URL>`, Python SDK `ScrapeOptions` and `Scraper` accept `proxy: str`, and REST API supports explicit upstream proxies.
   - Comprehensive proxy protocol support: `http://`, `https://`, `socks5://`, and **`socks5h://`** (remote hostname resolution on the proxy server), fully supporting TUN and fake-IP environments (Clash, Sing-box).

2. **🛡️ Granular SSRF CIDR Subnet Whitelisting**:
   - Replaces the legacy binary `allow_private_network` with a high-performance, zero-dependency bitmask CIDR evaluator (`IpCidr`) supporting IPv4 and IPv6.
   - CLI adds `--allow-cidr <CIDR>`, configuration adds `allow_cidrs = [...]`, and Python `Scraper` accepts `allow_cidrs=["198.18.0.0/15", "10.0.0.0/8"]`.
   - Out-of-the-box support for benchmarking networks, internal enterprise intranets, and RFC 2544 fake-IP ranges (`198.18.0.0/15`).

3. **🔌 Pip Package MCP Entry Point**:
   - `pagesift-mcp` is now installed as a top-level executable entry point alongside `pagesift` when installed via pip.
   - Exposes `python -m pagesift.mcp` and `python -m pagesift mcp` for cross-platform model context protocol server execution.
   - Native PyO3 binding `run_mcp(transport, port)` connects directly to the underlying high-performance Rust MCP server.

4. **🔬 Precision Academic Boilerplate Pruning (arXiv / Preprints)**:
   - Strips lingering non-article boilerplate embedded inside `<main>` containers on academic sites like arXiv (`1706.03762`).
   - Automatically cleans arXivLabs tabs, CORE Recommender, HuggingFace demo widgets, bookmarks, and author endorser blocks, leaving pure paper title, author list, abstract, metadata, and submission history.

5. **⚡ Incremental Scraping & HTTP 304 Conditional Requests**:
   - Added `if_none_match` (ETag) and `if_modified_since` parameters to Python `ScrapeOptions` and `Scraper.scrape`.
   - Python `Document` exposes `not_modified: bool` (`True` when server responds with HTTP 304, with `status_code == 304` and zero body parsing overhead).
   - Published exhaustive practical documentation [docs/incremental-collection.md](https://github.com/YOLOW92/pagesift/blob/v0.51.0/docs/incremental-collection.md) covering Python, Node.js, Rust, and REST API.

---

## 📦 Upgrading to 0.51.0

### Rust (Cargo.toml)
```toml
[dependencies]
pagesift = "0.51.0"
```

### Python (PyPI)
```bash
pip install --upgrade pagesift==0.51.0
pagesift-mcp --help
```

### Node.js (npm)
```bash
npm install @pagesift/node@0.51.0
```

### Docker (GHCR)
```bash
docker pull ghcr.io/yolow92/pagesift:0.51.0
```

# pagesift 0.40.0

A high-performance Rust web scraping and content extraction engine for AI agents and LLM pipelines. All workspace crates and native distributions move from 0.30.0 to **0.40.0** together.

## What changes

- **Dual-Protocol Firecrawl v1 & v2 Architecture:** Full dual-protocol routing in `crates/pagesift-api/src/firecrawl/` with complete backwards compatibility. Supports both `V1FirecrawlApp` (`/v1/scrape`, `/v1/crawl`, `/v1/batch/scrape`, `/v1/map`) and `FirecrawlApp` (`/v2/scrape`, `/v2/crawl`, etc.) with zero-overhead routing, parameter normalization, and asynchronous state machines.
- **Jina Reader Protocol Adapter:** Dedicated Jina Reader compatibility layer (`crates/pagesift-api/src/jina/`) offering clean URL extraction (`GET /r/{*url}` or `POST /r`), Server-Sent Events (`Accept: text/event-stream`), and raw Markdown streaming output for drop-in LLM Agent integration without configuration.
- **Unrestricted Multi-Core Concurrency & Massive Throughput:** Achieved **3,525 pages/sec** on 16-thread multi-core extraction benchmarks (0.57s for 2,008 WCXB pages, **14.6× faster** than `rs-trafilatura` and **18.4× faster** than Python `trafilatura`) with 53.8% less memory.
- **Hard 12 GiB RAM Defense Under Chaos:** In a 50,000-page adversarial crawl comparison, `Spider 2.53.9` suffered severe memory leaks and was terminated by the 12 GiB watchdog after consuming 11.7 GiB RSS. PageSift completed 48,433 pages in 17.76s (**2,727 pages/sec**) with peak memory bounded at **447.5 MB** (26× less RAM). In the 100,000-page synthetic chaos origin test (spider traps, 150-level nested DOMs, 503 backpressure, 429 rate limits), PageSift handled 3,000 backpressure events with zero crashes, strictly bounding peak RSS to **67.9 MB**.
- **olmOCR-Bench Leading PDF Extraction:** Evaluated against 500 academic papers, achieving **71.0%** pass rate (vs `pymupdf4llm` 64.4%), **44.3%** LaTeX mathematical formula accuracy (vs 0.0% for all Python competitors), and **3.4 ms/page** latency (**94× faster**).
- **Sub-Millisecond DOM Self-Healing & Structural Extraction:** In 500 adversarial chaos mutation scenarios, PageSift's business-anchor healing engine achieved **93.8% (469/500)** recall and **0.0% false positives** in **24.6 µs**. Relocated 200-level deeply nested DOM paths in 909 µs with zero stack overflow. Schema.org structured data extraction completed in **80.1 µs/page** (**41.5× faster** than `extruct`).
- **High-Performance RAG Chunking & Charset Detection:** Token-aware chunking achieved R@1000 = **0.895** at **21.5 ms** (**20.8× faster** than `semchunk`). Multi-byte encoding detector achieved **74.4%** accuracy on 3,138 legacy corpus files (**+5.5%** over `chardet`), **99.7%** on Unicode, at **0.45 ms/file**.
- **Codebase Modularization & Safety:** All new and modified Rust modules strictly adhere to `<= 500 lines` per file. `pagesift-api` preserves strict `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`.

## Migration

No breaking changes for existing HTTP `/v2` or MCP users.
- Users wishing to use official Firecrawl Python/Node SDKs v1 or v2 can point their `base_url` directly to PageSift.
- LLM agents requiring Jina Reader endpoints can target `http://<host>:<port>/r/<target_url>`.
- Rust crate users upgrading from 0.30.0 should update dependency version strings to `0.40.0`.
